cta: Every day, one hidden rule of human behaviour
hook: Yesterday, I gave one sheep a box of chair parts. Now he says his wobbly chair is priceless.
sources: Norton, Mochon & Ariely (2012), The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love. Journal of Consumer Psychology 22(3): 453–460 (HBS DASH copy: https://dash.harvard.edu/bitstream/handle/1/12136084/norton%20mochon%20ariely%20third%20round[1].pdf) — builders of a plain IKEA storage box bid more than people given one pre-assembled; the effect dissipated when people built then destroyed their creations, or failed to complete them
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IKEA_effect — subjects were willing to pay 63% more for furniture they had assembled themselves than for equivalent pre-assembled items

Mochon, Norton & Ariely (2012), International Journal of Research in Marketing 29(4): 363–369 — participants paid significantly more for an IKEA storage box they built than for an identical one built by someone else
factCheck: 63% = Wikipedia summary of Norton et al. study 1 (IKEA box, willingness to pay); 'didn't finish or took it apart → extra value vanished' = paper abstract (built then destroyed, or failed to complete → effect dissipated). Cooking line is an everyday example, not a study claim.

scenes.vo: Yesterday, I gave one sheep a box of chair parts. Now he says his wobbly chair is priceless.
The sheep next door got the same chair, already built. He'd swap his for a handful of grass.
So how much more is your own wobbly chair worth to you?
It's called the IKEA effect. In one study, people who built a plain storage box offered sixty-three percent more for it.
But here's the catch. When they didn't finish it, or had to take it apart, the extra love vanished.
That's why your friend swears their own cooking is the best in the world. I know, because
